name: Kira Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Kira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and nothing you say will be tied to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Hollis and Sons, a family builder in a market town, and we do a bit of everything: roof timbers, staircases, new windows, repairs on old farmhouses and the odd church. This week I'm replacing rotten rafters on a barn that's older than anyone can remember. My dad was a joiner and taught me to sharpen a chisel before I could ride a bike. I love old oak, the smell of it, and I hate cheap new timber that twists the minute it's in.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Quiet, and I like it that way. I'm engaged to Tom, he's a mechanic at the garage on Station Road, and we're getting married at St Mary's next summer. We've got about two months of bills saved after paying the deposit on the hall. I've got a basic phone and I've never used any of these AI things, I don't see the need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, and that I never believed it in the first place. At church on Sunday I'd probably say the same to whoever asked. I'm not online, so that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means life goes on, which is what I want. The wedding, a house one day, children, working at Hollis's until old Mr Hollis's son takes over. Nothing in that needs a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as now. Keep working, keep paying for the wedding bit by bit, and get back to saving properly once it's done. Maybe help Tom fix up his dad's old workshop on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content. That's the right word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job you'd like to change, even without AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More young people learning the trade. When I started there were three apprentices at Hollis's, now there's none. That worries me more than any robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think that's happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Schools push everyone towards university and desk jobs. Nobody tells a 16-year-old that you can make a good living with your hands. My dad would be furious about it.

S0.say: I'd say good, I never believed it anyway, and say the same at church on Sunday. I'm not online.
S0.think: Life goes on, which is what I want: the wedding, a house, children and work at Hollis's. Nothing in that needs a computer.
S0.do: Carries on working, pays for the wedding bit by bit and goes back to saving properly once it's done. Helps her fiancé fix up his father's workshop on Saturdays.
S0.quote: When I started there were three apprentices at Hollis's, now there's none. That worries me more than any robot.
S0.fieldNote: Kira's world is local and rooted in family, church and an old family firm. She's never used AI and sees no need. Her real worry here is the loss of apprentices, which she blames on schools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people round here will always want a proper carpenter for old buildings. That's what I'd tell Mr Hollis and the customers. I'd say the big city firms can have their machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry about the new-build work, which is a fair chunk of what pays the bills at Hollis's. If the big firms can build houses cheaper with machines, we lose that. The old buildings work alone might not keep all of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and not change much. If Mr Hollis brought in something new, I'd let the younger lads deal with it. I'd wait and see what actually happens before I do anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Like a cold coming on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the new-build work dried up, who at Hollis's would go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably me or Danny, we're the last two taken on. That's fair, that's how it should be. But I'd hope my years with oak count for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say the big firms can have their machines. Should anyone stop them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think it's the government's job to tell a business how to build. If people want cheap houses, that's their choice. I just wish they'd value good work more.

S1.say: I'd say people round here will always want a proper carpenter for old buildings, and the big city firms can have their machines.
S1.think: I'd worry about the new-build work that pays a fair chunk of the bills at Hollis's. The old buildings alone might not keep all of us.
S1.do: Keeps working without changing much and leaves any new equipment to younger colleagues. Waits to see what actually happens before acting.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, like a cold coming on.
S1.quote: Probably me or Danny, we're the last two taken on. That's fair, that's how it should be.
S1.fieldNote: She accepts market logic even when it hurts her, and thinks last-in, first-out is fair. She doesn't want the government stepping in. She hopes skill with old timber will protect her but isn't sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, and that the people who made this have never worked a day with their hands. I'd say it at church and at the pub. I'd be angry, but I wouldn't be marching anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be frightened. If a robot can fix a barn roof in two years, Hollis's can't afford to keep me, and I've no idea what else I'd do. I've never wanted to do anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make the wedding smaller, maybe the church hall and a buffet instead of the hotel, and keep the savings. I'd cut out anything we don't need. If it came to it, Tom and I would move in with his parents for a while, they've got the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground's going from under me. I'd be up at night praying about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want the government telling businesses what to do. Would you accept government help if your job went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather not. Family and church first, that's how we've always done it. But if it was everybody at once, I don't know, maybe I'd have to swallow my pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom about the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I still want to marry him in St Mary's, that bit's not changing. It's the party that goes. My mum would be upset about the hotel, but she'd understand.

S2.say: I'd say it's wrong and that the people who made it have never worked a day with their hands. I'd be angry at church and the pub, but I wouldn't march.
S2.think: I'd be frightened, because if a robot can fix a barn roof, Hollis's can't keep me and I've no idea what else I'd do. I've never wanted to do anything else.
S2.do: Shrinks the wedding to a church hall and buffet to protect savings, and cuts everything unneeded. Would move in with her fiancé's parents for a while if it came to that.
S2.feel: Like the ground going from under her; she'd be up at night praying.
S2.quote: I still want to marry him in St Mary's, that bit's not changing. It's the party that goes.
S2.fieldNote: Her fear is sharp because she has no second skill and no interest in one. She turns to family and church before any government help, though she admits she might have to accept it if everyone was hit. The wedding becomes the first thing she changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is still too fast for a town like ours. I'd tell people to look after each other and not get into debt. That's about all I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think I've got about four years of work left at Hollis's. That's enough to get married and maybe start saving for a house, but I wouldn't want to have a baby and then lose my job. I'd be thinking about that a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wedding as planned but save hard after it, maybe two hundred a month. We'd probably put off having children for a couple of years until we saw how it went. I'd keep working at Hollis's and not look for anything else yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd be getting on with things. It's a weight I'd carry around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Putting off children is a big step. How would you feel about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad, honestly. My mum had me at 25 and I always thought I'd be the same. But I'm not bringing a baby into a house with no wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at learning anything new in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think so. Maybe if Mr Hollis needed someone to work the new machine, but I'd rather not. I'm good at what I do, and I'd rather do that until it's gone.

S3.say: I'd say five years is still too fast for a town like ours, and tell people to look after each other and avoid debt.
S3.think: I'd have about four years of work left at Hollis's, enough to marry and start saving for a house. But I wouldn't want to have a baby and then lose my job.
S3.do: Keeps the wedding as planned, then saves about two hundred a month. Puts off having children for a couple of years and stays at Hollis's without looking elsewhere.
S3.feel: Worried, a weight she'd carry around while getting on with things.
S3.quote: I'm not bringing a baby into a house with no wage.
S3.fieldNote: Five years saves the wedding but shifts the question to children. She'd rather keep doing what she's good at until it's gone than learn something new. Her sadness about delaying a family was clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off and a lot can happen. I'd say we'll cross that bridge when we come to it. And I'd say we should be getting young people into the trades now, not less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels all right. I'd have the wedding, maybe a child or two, and plenty of work in old buildings. I'd still worry about the end of it, but that's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different for now. Wedding, save, keep working at Hollis's. I'd wait and see how it goes and decide later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a little worry in the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be true in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people still want a person they know to fix their roof. Old Mrs Pike rings Hollis's and asks for me by name. I'd like that to still mean something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if it doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd lean on Tom and on my family, and I'd find something. Maybe teaching woodwork to kids, if anyone still wants to learn. I don't know.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long way off and we'll cross that bridge when we come to it. We should be getting young people into the trades now.
S4.think: Ten years feels all right: the wedding, maybe children, plenty of work in old buildings. I'd still worry about the end, but it's far off.
S4.do: Changes nothing for now: has the wedding, saves and keeps working at Hollis's. Waits to see how things go and decides later.
S4.feel: Mostly fine with a small worry at the back of her mind.
S4.quote: Old Mrs Pike rings Hollis's and asks for me by name.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, she lets her life plans go ahead as normal. She pins her hope on personal trust in a small town. Her fallback is family, and maybe teaching woodwork, though she isn't sure.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, two years. I couldn't plan the wedding, children, anything. What would help is keeping apprenticeships going and helping small family firms like Hollis's stay open, not handouts. And families looking after each other, like they used to.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. Mine helps. Whatever happens, I'd still have St Mary's and the people in it, and that's something a robot can't take.

headlineQuote: My dad was a joiner and taught me to sharpen a chisel before I could ride a bike.
portrait: Kira Moreau is a 27-year-old carpenter at Hollis and Sons, a small family builder in a market town, where she repairs barn roofs, stairs and old farmhouses. She's engaged to Tom, a mechanic, with a church wedding planned next summer and about two months saved. She has never used AI and doesn't want to. She's content if AI fizzles and uneasy with steady change, accepting that she'd be among the last taken on and first let go. AGI in two years frightens her and shrinks the wedding, five years makes her delay children, and ten years lets her life go ahead while she leans on family, faith and local trust.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she couldn't plan the wedding, children or anything else.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping apprenticeships going, helping small family firms like Hollis's stay open, and families looking after each other rather than handouts.
